In the iPhone 18 Pro, Apple has taken the next step toward its long-term vision of turning the iPhone into a single piece of glass: embedding the Face ID module beneath the display.

Pulling this off without letting the Face ID array show through the screen, or compromising display quality in that area, requires some clever engineering…

Jony Ive once described his long-term vision for the iPhone's design as a single piece of glass. Even though he has left the company, that goal has carried forward. Apple ultimately wants to hide all the technology that currently takes up screen real estate—including Face ID and the front-facing camera—underneath the display.

The iPhone 18 Pro is the first to get partway there, but it wasn't easy. Face ID requires a TrueDepth module that both emits and receives infrared light, and infrared cannot pass through the display's pixels.

Apple needed to create enough space between the pixels for infrared light to pass through, without introducing any visible flaws on the screen. To do this, the company's engineers set about designing a brand new pixel layout that widens the gaps between pixels without noticeably affecting display quality in that area.

iFixit has shown off the pixel pattern using a microscope, and Apple confirmed to me that the overall pixel density in the module area has been cut in half. That could have created a second problem: halving the pixel density could make that part of the screen noticeably dimmer, so Apple has boosted the brightness of those pixels to compensate. In addition, there's reportedly an infrared filter that blocks visible light from passing through the gaps between pixels, further hiding the internal components.

The result is stunning. In everyday use, the TrueDepth camera array is essentially impossible to spot, even if you stare at it intently. Even using macro photography, with different screen colors and lighting conditions, I couldn't get it to show up. That's not to say it's completely undetectable—iFixit's microscope images show it—but rather that in day-to-day use, you will absolutely not notice it's there.

For now, this breakthrough allows the Dynamic Island to shrink, which in turn supports three Live Activities displayed simultaneously instead of two. On future iPhone models, the front-facing camera will also be hidden under the display. This is technically already possible, but the image quality loss it would cause is still beyond what Apple is willing to accept. It's only a matter of time before that gets sorted out.
